title: Exploring public perceptions of dementia on Twitter (X): a cross-cultural analysis
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of dementia-related tweets in English and Thai (May 2017 - April 2021) in which every tweet was manually assigned one topic, one of which is an explicit 'misinformation' category. The paper reports the share of tweets in that category with full denominators: 4,683 (49.2%) of 9,511 Thai tweets and 179 (1.8%) of 10,062 English tweets. That is a share of items in a sample judged inaccurate by expert coders, i.e. CONTENT prevalence. See the judgement call in the row notes: the 'misinformation' label here means incorrect use of the term 'dementia' (e.g. a healthy young person saying 'must be the dementia'), which is inaccurate health content but not a false claim about the wider world.

estimates.country: Thailand (Thai-language tweets; "สมองเสื่อม" / "#สมองเสื่อม")
estimates.measure_type: % of Thai-language dementia tweets whose coded topic was misinformation
estimates.value_raw: misinformation was the most prevalent (4,683 [49.2%]) in Thai
estimates.denominator: 9,511 Thai-language tweets containing "สมองเสื่อม" or "#สมองเสื่อม" (dementia), retweets excluded, duplicates removed - all Thai tweets retrieved in the window
estimates.definition: A tweet counted in the numerator if manual coders assigned 'misinformation' as its single most relevant topic, i.e. the term dementia was applied inaccurately (Table 2 exemplar: "เมื่อกี้หัวโขกกำแพงดังมาก ผมสมองเสื่อมแล้ว" / "Just now, my head banged against the wall so loud. I have dementia."). Topics are mutually exclusive: "The most relevant topic was selected in cases where a tweet contained multiple topics." Figurative expressions, jokes and stigma are separate categories.
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition is given; misinformation is one of the coded topic categories ("advertisements, advocacy, public health or policy, information, stigma, joke, figurative expressions, misinformation, and unidentified"), and the paper describes it as an inaccurate use of the term dementia: "Different inappropriate uses of 'dementia' were observed."
estimates.source_quote: However, we found misinformation was the most prevalent (4,683 [49.2%]) in Thai, but only 179 [1.8%] examples of it were found in English ( p < 0.001) (Figure 1 and Table 3 ).
estimates.page_loc: Results 3.1 'Topic analysis and stigmatized tweets'; Figure 1 and Table 3
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Manual coding by a clinical/linguistic team: the first 480 tweets per language (10 per month) were coded simultaneously by three researchers (an internist, a geriatrician and a linguist) with "substantial agreement" on interrater reliability reported in Table S1; the remaining tweets were then coded by a single researcher (S.S.). Coding followed a predefined stepwise scheme (Figure S1) on syntactic and semantic features. Exact kappa values are in the supplement, which is not in this text.
estimates.moderator_quote: This cross-sectional study utilized data obtained from the Twitter Application Programming Interface for Academic Research, focusing on dementia-related tweets in English and Thai from May 1, 2017 to April 30, 2021. ... Tweets containing the words "dementia," "#dementia," and their Thai equivalents ("สมองเสื่อม" and "#สมองเสื่อม") were retrieved.
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL for the adjudicator (the reason borderline=true): the paper's 'misinformation' category is misuse of a clinical term - typically a person without dementia attributing ordinary forgetfulness or a bump on the head to 'dementia'. It is coded against clinical knowledge by expert coders and the paper calls it misinformation, so it satisfies 'inaccurate health content'; but it is not a false claim about the world of the kind most prevalence studies count, and the very high Thai figure (49.2%) is driven by this colloquial misuse. If the review restricts CONTENT to false claims about external facts, both rows in this paper should be re-typed or dropped. Country is inferred from tweet language: the study reports no user geolocation (its own limitation: 'The absence of user demographic data (eg, country, gender, age)'). year = 2019, the midpoint of the four-year window (full window in date).

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language tweets, no user geolocation)
estimates.measure_type: % of English-language dementia tweets whose coded topic was misinformation
estimates.value_raw: only 179 [1.8%] examples of it were found in English
estimates.denominator: 10,062 English-language tweets containing "dementia" or "#dementia", randomly sampled month by month from the 4,641,937 English dementia tweets in the window (0.22%), retweets excluded, duplicates removed
estimates.definition: A tweet counted in the numerator if manual coders assigned 'misinformation' as its single most relevant topic (Table 2 exemplar: "I moved off campus at 20 and I'm not even 27 yet must be the dementia.").
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition; 'misinformation' is one of the mutually exclusive coded topics, described as an inappropriate/inaccurate use of the term dementia.
estimates.source_quote: However, we found misinformation was the most prevalent (4,683 [49.2%]) in Thai, but only 179 [1.8%] examples of it were found in English ( p < 0.001) (Figure 1 and Table 3 ). FIGURE 1 Percentage of topic analysis according to English (A) and Thai (B) tweets. Other topic analysis for English tweets: misinformation 1.8%, advocacy 1.6%, public health or policy 1.5%, advertisement 1.4%, unidentified 1.3%, and <1% for jokes and figurative expressions.
estimates.page_loc: Results 3.1 'Topic analysis and stigmatized tweets'; Figure 1 caption
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same coding procedure as the Thai row: 480 tweets per language triple-coded by an internist, a geriatrician and a linguist with substantial interrater agreement (Table S1), remainder coded by one researcher.
estimates.moderator_quote: Because the number of English tweets significantly exceeded the Thai tweets, we employed random sampling using the NumPy package (version 1.21.2) to select a subset of English tweets that were equal in number to the Thai tweets each month to ensure a balanced dataset for analysis. ... The English tweets accounted for 0.22% of all English tweets during the study period (4,641,937 tweets).
estimates.notes: Same construct caveat as the Thai row (see its notes). The English sample is a random monthly subsample of the full English keyword corpus, so the estimate generalises to English dementia tweets in the window; sampling_frame stays keyword_topical (random within a single-issue keyword corpus) and denom_selection is left blank because the corpus is not rank-truncated or curated. No country is recoverable: language only.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) '"Dementia" was used accurately in 39.0% of English tweets' (abstract) is the 'general information' topic share, 3,927 [39.0%] - an accuracy/topic share, not a misinformation share, so no row. (2) Subgroup misinformation shares by user type (Table 3-style breakdown) were not extracted because subgroups are not the paper's headline: notably 'misinformation was found among Thai health personnel (7 [6.1%]), but we did not see this phenomenon in English (0)', and further cells of 0-2.2% for other user types. An adjudicator who wants a professional-population row could add Thai health personnel 7/115 = 6.1%, population_scope=professional. (3) Stigma (English 3,910 [38.9%], Thai 2,147 [22.6%]) and negative sentiment (English 44.2%, Thai 81.3%) are stigma/tone constructs, not veracity, so no rows (they would be OTHER at best). (4) 'The English tweets accounted for 0.22% of all English tweets during the study period (4,641,937 tweets)' is a sampling fraction, not a misinformation share. (5) Interrater reliability values live in Table S1 (supplement) and are described only as 'substantial agreement' in this text, so the exact kappa could not be recorded.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of Twitter (X) Academic Research API data, 1 May 2017 - 30 April 2021, tweets containing 'dementia'/'#dementia' and the Thai equivalents; retweets excluded, text preprocessed, duplicates removed; all Thai tweets kept (9,511) and English tweets randomly subsampled month by month to match (10,062 of 4,641,937, i.e. 0.22%). Each tweet manually assigned one user type, one topic (including a misinformation category) and one sentiment; first 480 tweets per language coded simultaneously by three researchers (internist, geriatrician, linguist) with 'substantial' interrater agreement reported in Table S1, remainder single-coded by S.S. No user geolocation or demographics (acknowledged limitation); country is inferred from tweet language. Ethics approval COA. MURA2023/207.
